Day of the Dead history for sleep: two slow hours in one real town, San Andrés Mixquic, on the southern edge of Mexico City, across five hundred years. We begin when Mixquic was an island in Lake Chalco and its people kept summer months for the dead, then follow All Saints and All Souls, sugar lambs and sugar skulls, Posada's lady in the big hat, and a family's ofrenda tonight. A bedtime story for grown-ups, told gently and with respect.

In November 1841, a visitor walking under the arcades of Mexico City heard the old women at their stalls calling, "Skulls, girls, skulls!" The skulls were made of sugar.

What is the Day of the Dead?

The Day of the Dead, usually called Día de Muertos in Mexico (Día de los Muertos is also used), is a time when families remember the people they have loved and welcome them home for a little while. It is kept around the Catholic feasts of All Saints on 1 November and All Souls on 2 November, and in many places it begins in the last days of October.

Families clean and decorate graves, build an ofrenda at home with photographs, candles, water, food and marigolds, and lay a path of petals so the dead can find their way. UNESCO recognises it as an Indigenous festivity, as practised by the Indigenous communities of Mexico, and describes it as a fusion of pre-Hispanic rites and Catholic feasts. It isn't a night for frights. There is grief, and also food, old stories and quiet laughter.

Where did the Day of the Dead come from?

Historians still discuss it, and the honest answer is: from two worlds. The Mexica (Aztecs) kept two months linked with the dead, Miccailhuitontli, the little feast of the dead, and Hueymiccailhuitl, the great feast. In 1519 they fell in late July and August, with flowers and food offered in temples and homes. The Spanish brought All Saints and All Souls, with bells, candles, bread and burial in churchyards.

Around 1580 the Dominican friar Diego Durán saw offerings for children on All Saints and for grown-ups on All Souls, and wondered, without daring to affirm it, whether the old feasts had moved inside the new ones. Elsa Malvido traced most of the customs to Catholic Europe; Ruben Cordova sees a memory of the two old months in that split between children and adults. The popular story that kindly priests moved the festival to November has no real evidence behind it.

Where did the Mexica believe the dead went?

For the Mexica, where you went depended less on how you had lived than on how you died. Warriors who fell in battle went east to the house of the sun, and women who died giving birth joined the sun in the west. People who drowned or were struck by lightning went to Tlalocan, the green land of the rain god. Most people went to Mictlan, the land of the dead, ruled by Mictlantecuhtli and Mictecacihuatl.

The road there, the old accounts recorded by Sahagún say, took four years, ending at a broad river, Chiconahuapan, the nine waters, where a small yellow dog carried its master across. Some later pictures show nine levels of Mictlan; the sources differ. Families made offerings at eighty days and on each anniversary for four years. The idea of a yearly visit home, so central today, grew later, where this world met the Catholic one.

What goes on a Day of the Dead ofrenda?

There's no single right way. An ofrenda can have one step or several, on a table or, in Mixquic's old way, on a woven reed mat called a petate. Saints, the Virgin of Guadalupe and a cross often stand at the back. Then come candles to light the way; a glass of water, because people say the dead are thirsty after the long journey; a dish of salt; copal incense in a clay burner; fruit, tamales and pan de muerto, the bread of the dead.

In Mixquic the children's things come first: sweets, milk and small clay toys, with white flowers. The next day come marigolds for the grown-ups, their favourite food and drink, perhaps mole or pulque, and a photograph. Sugar skulls carry names, papel picado flutters overhead, and a path of petals leads from the door. Afterwards the food is shared with the living, never wasted.

Why are there sugar skulls?

Sugar arrived with the Spanish, and so did alfeñique, a craft of shaping sweets from sugar paste that had reached Spain with the Moors of al-Andalus. In the 1760s the Capuchin friar Francisco de Ajofrín saw a thousand little sugar figures sold under Mexico City's merchants' arcade before All Saints: lambs and sheep, coffins, priests, nuns and gentlemen on horseback. There were no skulls in his list.

By the autumn of 1841, Frances Calderón de la Barca found the booths filled with sugar skulls, temptingly ranged in grinning rows, and old women calling, "Skulls, niñas, skulls!" Today sugar skulls with names piped across the forehead go on the ofrenda, and they're given to the living too, as a joke and a kindness at once. The city of Toluca holds a whole alfeñique fair every year.

Who is La Catrina?

She began as a joke about a hat. Around 1910 the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada drew a woman's skull under a huge hat piled with flowers and ostrich plumes, mocking people who tried too hard to look European and fashionable. The picture was first printed in 1913, after his death, on a broadsheet that called her a garbancera, a street seller of chickpeas; the verse wasn't his.

In 1946 and 1947 Diego Rivera put her at the centre of his mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda, with a full body, a long white dress and a feathered serpent for a boa, holding Posada's arm. The name Catrina is usually credited to Rivera, though not everyone agrees. She isn't an ancient Aztec goddess, or Mictecacihuatl in modern clothes. She's a twentieth-century figure, and that story is interesting enough on its own.

What is the Alumbrada in Mixquic?

San Andrés Mixquic, an old lake town in Tláhuac on the southern edge of Mexico City, keeps a careful calendar for its dead. People say they are first invited on 29 September, when graves are cleaned and painted. Then, as the town's chronicler told a university researcher: 28 October for those who died by accident, 30 October for children who died before baptism, noon on 31 October for the other children, and 1 November for the grown-ups. On the evening of the first, children go from door to door as campaneros, ringing a hand bell.

The Alumbrada, the lighting, is the night of 2 November. From about six in the evening until about midnight, families light candles on the graves around the old church of San Andrés, sit together, share coffee and bread, and tell stories. The next day they share out the ofrenda, which they call dar la calavera.

0:00:00Intro · 330 words

In the autumn of 1841, a visitor walking under the arcades of Mexico City heard old women calling from their stalls, "Skulls, girls, skulls!" The skulls were made of sugar.

At dusk, beside the water, a family's altar glows: bright paper banners overhead, small candles, a carpet of orange marigold petals, and one large sugar skull, painted with flowers in orange, turquoise and pink.

This is Dreaming Ages. Over the next two hours, we'll walk the marigold paths of the Day of the Dead, Día de los Muertos, or simply Día de Muertos, from the old island town of Mixquic to a family's vigil tonight.

Nothing loud, nothing sudden. Just a slow voice, the smell of warm bread, and a great many small candles.

So settle in, and let your breathing slow.

It's the second evening of November, in San Andrés Mixquic, an old lake town on the southern edge of Mexico City.

Intro

The sky over the canals is turning from gold to violet. Along the lane to the church, people walk slowly with their arms full: bundles of orange flowers, covered baskets, a folding chair, a thermos of something hot.

Tonight we'll stay in this one town across five hundred years. We'll begin in a late summer when Mixquic was an island in a lake, and its people spoke Nahuatl. We'll watch the first church bells ring over the water, walk under the old arcades of the capital, and come back to a family keeping watch beside a grave.

When something is uncertain or imagined, I'll say so as we go.

This isn't a frightening story. It's about families remembering the people they've loved, and welcoming them home for a little while. Historians still discuss how much of it comes from the old Mexica world and how much came across the ocean. We'll hear both sides. Most agree it grew from both, and kept growing.

Now, let's go back five hundred years, to the same place, in late summer.

0:03:10An Island in Late Summer: Mixquic and Tenochtitlan · 1,260 words

It's early morning, around the year 1500, and a thin mist is lying on the water.

The lake here is called Chalco. It's shallow and fresh, fed by springs at the foot of the hills to the south. Far to the northwest, beyond more water and more towns, stands the great island city of Tenochtitlan, the heart of the Mexica world. From here you can't see it. You can see the mountains, though, which ring the whole valley like the rim of a bowl. And to the southeast, when the mist thins, two great volcanoes rise above everything, one often trailing a plume of pale smoke, the other long and white along its top, like a figure lying asleep.

Mixquic sits on an island in this lake. Its name is usually read as "at the mesquite tree", and in the old painted books its sign is a thorny mesquite. You may hear that it means "place of death", but that's a modern story. It's an old town, and for a long time its more powerful neighbours fought over it, one after another. Then, in the 1400s, in the reign of the Mexica ruler Itzcóatl, Mexica armies came. The painted books list Mixquic among his conquests. Since then, like the other conquered towns of the valley, it has sent tribute to Tenochtitlan.

All around the island, the farmers have made fields out of the lake itself. They're called chinampas. Long, narrow beds of earth, built up from layers of mud and reeds and rotted plants, held in place by stakes and by the roots of willows planted along their edges. Between them run canals, straight and still, just wide enough for a canoe. From above, the whole island looks as if it's set in a great green comb laid on the water.

The chinampas are wonderfully rich. Their soil is always damp from below, and every so often the farmers scoop fresh black mud up from the canal bottoms and spread it over the beds. Here they grow maize, and beans, and squash, and chiles, and tomatoes, and amaranth, and flowers. Many, many flowers.

It's the rainy season now. For weeks, almost every afternoon, the clouds have built up over the mountains, dark and heavy, and then rolled across the valley in a long, drumming rain. By evening the sky clears, and the frogs start up in the canals. And in the mornings, like this one, everything is washed and cool, and the mist rises off the water in slow curls.

The maize is tall. Taller than a man, in the best beds, with long green leaves that rustle when the breeze comes off the lake, and tassels on top just turning pale. The cobs inside the husks are still young and soft. Harvest is a long way off yet.

Let's follow one canal, slowly, toward a house at the end of it.

It's a low house of adobe brick, plastered and whitened, with a roof of thatch. There's a little courtyard in front, swept clean, and a round, domed sweat bath to one side. Beside the door, a turkey is scratching in the dust. The family's canoe is tied up at the edge of the canal, a long dugout made from a single tree.

In the doorway sits an old woman, wrapped in a cotton mantle against the morning cool. Her name, in our story, is Citlalin. It means star. She's imagined, like everyone we'll meet in Mixquic tonight. She's a grandmother many times over, and she's lived beside this water all her life.

Beside her, half awake, is her grandson Tochtli. His name means rabbit, because he was born on a day of the Rabbit, and he's about ten. He's been told that today he can help her with something important.

Today the flowers have to be gathered.

The month that's beginning now has a lovely name. It's called Tlaxochimaco, which means something like "the giving of flowers". That name comes from a Franciscan friar, Bernardino de Sahagún, who spent decades, later in the 1500s, gathering what the Mexica could still tell him about their old festivals. His helpers wrote down that, at this time of year, people went out across the countryside looking for every flower they could find. Mountain flowers, water lilies, all kinds of flowers with names we can only guess at in English. And among them, again and again, a round, ruffled flower of deep yellow and orange.

In Nahuatl it's called cempoalxochitl. The word means "twenty flower", and people often understand it as "the flower of many petals". Today, in Spanish, it's cempasúchil. In English we'd call it a marigold. And in five hundred years' time, here in Mixquic, it will still be grown and sold by the armful, for the same season of remembering.

But we're getting ahead of ourselves. For now, it's just a flower Citlalin loves.

She stands, slowly, and Tochtli unties the canoe. She sits in the middle, and he takes the long pole and pushes off, the way his father showed him, leaning his weight into it and walking it back hand over hand. The canoe slides out along the canal without a sound.

The mist is lifting. Along the edges of the beds, white herons stand on one leg, watching the water. A kingfisher flashes past. In the next chinampa a man is already at work, bent over, his digging stick going in and out of the soft earth. He raises a hand to them. Citlalin raises hers back.

At the end of the family's own beds, beyond the maize, there's a long strip where the flowers grow. The marigolds are not yet at their fullest. Their great season comes later, as the rains end. But there are enough. Tochtli holds the canoe steady against the bank, and Citlalin leans out and picks them, one by one, laying them in a basket at her feet. The smell rises around them, sharp and green and a little bitter, unlike any other flower.

"Not too many from one plant," she says. "Leave some for later."

She picks other flowers too. White ones, and red ones, and pale yellow ones that grow at the water's edge. By the time the sun is fully up and the last of the mist is gone, the basket is heaped full, and Tochtli's arms are tired from the pole.

On the way home, they pass the temple of the town. It stands on a raised platform near the heart of the island, with steps up the front and a shrine on top. One day, a church will stand on this same ground. Already people are climbing those steps with flowers in their arms. Sahagún's helpers recorded that in the great city, the image of the Mexica patron god was decked with garlands of flowers at dawn, and then flowers were offered in the other temples, and in the houses of the lords. In a farming town like Mixquic, we can picture something humbler, in the same spirit. That part is imagined.

Back at the house, Citlalin sets the basket down in the shade, and sprinkles it with water from a jar, so the flowers will keep. Then she sits again in the doorway, and looks out at the canal, and the maize, and the mountains, as the morning warms.

Tochtli asks her why they need so many flowers this month.

She takes a long time to answer. And when she does, she doesn't talk about gods at all, at first. She talks about his grandfather.

0:12:29Two Months for the Dead: Mexica (Aztec) Festivals · 981 words

To understand why this month matters, we need to understand a little about time, as the Mexica kept it.

They had two great calendars, turning together like wheels. One was a sacred count of two hundred and sixty days, used for naming children and reading fortunes. Tochtli's name came from that one. The other was a year of three hundred and sixty five days, made of eighteen months of twenty days each, with five extra days at the end, which were thought to be unlucky. Nobody started anything new in those five days.

That solar year had no leap day. So, slowly, over many years, its months drifted against the real seasons, the way a clock drifts if no one ever winds it right. Historians have to work hard to say exactly when a given month fell. But in the year 1519, according to one careful reckoning, the two months we're talking about ran from late July to the end of August. High summer. The height of the rains. The maize growing tall.

And these two months, the ninth and the tenth of the year, were both connected with the dead.

The ninth month, the one that's beginning now in our story, had two names. One was Tlaxochimaco, the giving of flowers. The other was Miccailhuitontli. It's a long word, but it breaks into pieces. Micca means the dead. Ilhuitl means a feast day. And the little ending, tontli, makes it small. So it's the little feast of the dead. Or perhaps, the feast of the little dead.

That second meaning matters. A Dominican friar named Diego Durán, who grew up in New Spain and wrote about the old festivals in the 1570s, was told that this month was kept in memory of children who had died. The little dead. Then the next month, the tenth, was called Hueymiccailhuitl, the great feast of the dead. The feast for the grown-ups.

Scholars still discuss exactly what those names meant, and the old sources don't always agree. But it's a picture worth keeping in mind: a summer month for the children, and then a summer month for the adults.

What did people actually do? Here we have to be honest about where our knowledge comes from.

Almost everything we know about these festivals was written down after the Spanish conquest, mostly by Catholic friars like Sahagún and Durán. They were curious, and they were careful, and they talked to people who remembered. But they were also writing in order to root the old religion out. And by the time they asked, many of the priests who'd understood these rites most deeply were gone. So we see these festivals through a window that's a little cloudy, and that was made by people who didn't approve of what they saw.

Through that window, we see flowers. A great deal of flowers. Garlands and offerings in the temples. Feasting and singing and dancing. We see the tenth month built around a tall tree trunk, which was cut in the forest, carried into the city with great ceremony, and raised in a temple courtyard. A figure made of amaranth dough was set at the very top. At the end of the feast, young men raced each other up the trunk to bring the dough figure down, and the one who reached it first was greatly honoured. Durán says that a great amount of food and pulque, the milky drink made from the maguey plant, was laid around the foot of the pole.

These great festivals also included human sacrifice, as many Mexica festivals did. The friars describe it, and historians have studied it. We won't dwell on it here. It's part of the truth, and it's enough to say it plainly once.

For most families, in towns like Mixquic, the months of the dead would have meant something closer to home. We don't have a farmer's diary from the year 1500. Nobody wrote one. But we know from the sources that the dead were remembered with offerings, and that the living felt a duty to them. And in Citlalin's house, as the flowers wait in the shade, Citlalin is getting ready to do what grandmothers have always done.

In the corner of the main room, there's a low shelf against the wall, where the family keeps a few small clay figures, and a little bowl for burning incense. Today, Citlalin clears it, and wipes it down, and sets fresh flowers there. Then she lays out food. A few tortillas, still warm from the clay griddle. A small bowl of beans. A tamale wrapped in a corn husk. And a little cup of chocolate, frothed up the way her husband liked it.

Chocolate was precious in this world. The cacao beans came from far away in the hot lands to the south, and they were so valued that people used them as small change in the markets. A cup of it, poured out for someone who's gone, says a great deal.

Then she takes a pinch of pale resin from a small bag, and drops it onto a coal in the incense bowl. It's copal, the hardened sap of a tree, and it has been burned in offerings across this part of the world for a very long time. A thread of white smoke rises, and spreads, and the room fills with a sweet, piney scent.

Tochtli watches all this, sitting on a reed mat by the door.

"Will he come?" he asks.

"He'll know," says his grandmother.

Outside, the afternoon clouds are gathering over the mountains, as they do every day this time of year. Soon the rain will come, drumming on the thatch and dimpling the canals. But inside, the copal smoke drifts, and the marigolds glow orange on the shelf, and the little room is warm and dry and full of the smell of chocolate.

0:19:38The Long Road to Mictlan, the Mexica Land of the Dead · 1,003 words

That night, after the rain, the clouds break up, and a half moon comes out over the lake. Its light lies on the canals in long silver bars. The frogs are singing. The maize leaves drip.

Inside, the family is asleep on their mats, all except Citlalin, who sits by the hearth, where three stones hold the griddle over the last red coals. Tochtli is curled beside her, not quite asleep. And she tells him, in a low voice, about where the dead go.

What she tells him is drawn from what the Mexica told Sahagún, and from what historians have pieced together since. The details varied from place to place and from teller to teller, and we only have pieces. But the shape of it is this.

Where you went when you died depended less on how you had lived, and more on how you died.

Warriors who fell in battle, and those who died as offerings, went to the east, to the house of the sun. Every morning they walked with the sun as it rose, from the edge of the world up into the sky, singing and shaking their shields. After four years, the old accounts say, they came back to the earth as hummingbirds and butterflies, sipping from the flowers.

Women who died giving birth were honoured like warriors. They went to the west, and walked with the sun every afternoon, as it went down.

People who drowned, or were struck by lightning, or died of certain illnesses that were linked to water, went to a different place. It was called Tlalocan, the land of Tlaloc, the god of rain. And Tlalocan was a green and gentle country, where it was always summer, and the maize never failed, and there was no end to squash and beans and flowers.

But most people, the great majority of ordinary men and women who simply grew old, or fell ill, went somewhere else. They went to Mictlan, the place of the dead.

Mictlan lay far away, deep below, toward the north. It was ruled by a lord and a lady. The lord was called Mictlantecuhtli, the lord of the place of the dead. And the lady was Mictecacihuatl, the lady of the place of the dead. In the old stone carvings, they're shown as figures with fleshless faces. But they weren't thought of as cruel. They were the keepers of the dead, and the dead went to them in the end.

The road there was long. The old accounts recorded by Sahagún say that it took four years.

On the way, the dead had to pass a series of places. Two great mountains that knocked against each other. A road watched over by a serpent. Eight deserts. Eight hills. And a cold wind that cut like blades of obsidian, the black volcanic glass the Mexica used for their sharpest knives. Some later pictures show the land of the dead as nine levels, one below the other, while Sahagún's account reads more like a journey. The sources differ, and that's all right. Every family pictured it in its own way.

And at the end of the journey, the dead came to a broad river. Its name was Chiconahuapan, which means something like "the nine waters".

Here, Citlalin tells Tochtli, is where the little dog comes in.

When someone died, Sahagún writes, a small yellow dog was sent along with them, with a loose cotton cord tied around its neck. And when the dead person reached the great river, after their four years of walking, they would look across, and there, on the far bank, would be the dogs. And when a dog recognised its master, it would leap into the water and swim across, and carry them over on its back.

But not every dog would do. According to the story, a white dog would say, "I've just washed myself," and refuse to get wet. And a black dog would say, "I've just stained myself black," and refuse too. Only a yellow dog would carry you across.

Tochtli laughs at that, sleepily. Citlalin smiles.

Then she tells him the rest. While the dead person walked that long road, the family at home didn't forget them. At the funeral, the body was wrapped, and the things the dead would need were sent along with them. Then, at eighty days, the family made offerings again, and burned some of the person's belongings, so that they would reach them on the road. And they did it again after one year, and after two, and three, and four. On the fourth anniversary, it was believed, the journey was finally over. The dead had arrived. They were home, in their way.

Citlalin's husband died three years ago, in the dry season, of a fever. So this is the third summer she has made his offering. There's one more year to go.

She doesn't say this to Tochtli. She just watches the coals, and listens to the frogs, and to the water dripping from the thatch.

Historians would add a quiet note here. The four-year journey, the river and the yellow dog belong to the Mexica world, as Sahagún recorded it. The yearly visit home that families welcome today, with candles and bread and a path of petals, is a later story, where this world and another one, from across the ocean, meet. How much of that visit goes back to the Mexica, and how much came from Spain, is still discussed. We'll come to it.

For now, it's enough to sit here, by the three hearthstones, in a house on the edge of the lake, around the year 1500. The moon is high now. The flowers on the shelf are dark shapes against the night. The last thread of copal smoke has faded, but the scent is still there.

Tochtli is asleep. Citlalin lays a corner of her mantle over him.

In the Catholic year, the end of October and the start of November were a holy season. 1 November was the feast of All Saints, for all the holy people in heaven. And 2 November was All Souls, for everyone else. For all the ordinary dead, whom Christians prayed for, believing that their prayers could help the souls of the departed on their way to God.

All Souls had begun about a thousand years ago, at the great abbey of Cluny in France, when its abbot, Odilo, ordered his monks to pray for all the faithful departed on the day after All Saints. Over the next two centuries, the custom spread across Europe. By the time of the conquest, it was one of the best loved days of the year in Spain.

What did people in Spain do on these days? They went to Mass. The churches were hung with black. Bells were rung for the souls of the dead, often far into the night. And families took offerings to the church and to the graves. Bread, and wine, and candles, laid out in memory of the people they had lost. In many parts of Catholic Europe, people believed that on the night of All Souls, the dead came back for a little while to the homes they had known. The friars brought all of this. The bells, and the candles, and the bread, and the two holy days at the beginning of November. One had kept its feasts of the dead in the high summer, with flowers and food and copal smoke. The other kept them at the start of November, with candles and bread and bells.

What happened when they met is one of the most discussed questions in all of Mexican history. We'll come to the discussion. First, let's go back to Mixquic, and see.

He says the name means "the little feast of the dead", or "the feast of the little dead", and that as far as he could learn, it was a feast for children who had died. And then he adds something from his own experience.

On All Saints' Day, he writes, there's an offering in some places. And on All Souls' Day, another. He asked why they made it on All Saints, and people told him: for the children. That was how it was done in the old days, they said, and the custom had stayed. And would they offer again on All Souls? Yes, they said. For the grown-ups.

And so they did. Durán writes that he saw it plainly: the feasts of the dead, the little and the great, being kept. On one day, people offered money, and cacao, and wax, and birds, and fruit, and seeds in great quantity, and things to eat. And on the next day, he saw them do the same again.

He wasn't the only one to notice offerings at graves. In another part of his work, Durán describes a later month, called Quecholli, when people made little arrows, tied in fours with four small pine torches. They set them on the graves of the dead with two tamales, and left them there for a whole day before burning them at night. That month, in the wandering calendar, could fall in late October and November. But we should be careful not to make too much of that. The old months moved, and Durán was describing the Mexica past, not the colonial present.

Historians have been turning Durán's sentence over ever since.

Some read it as evidence that something of the old feasts survived. The split that Durán saw, children on 1 November and grown-ups on the second, is still kept across much of Mexico today. In most of Catholic Europe, 1 November is simply for the saints. So perhaps, they suggest, the memory of a feast for the little dead and a feast for the great dead found a new home on the old days of the Church.

Others point out how much of what we now call the Day of the Dead looks very like what people did in Spain. Food set out for the dead. A favourite dish for someone especially loved. Candles at the graves. A path marked with flowers so the souls could find their way home. Bread and sweets in the shapes of bones. One Mexican historian, Elsa Malvido, founded a workshop on the history of death at the national institute of anthropology and history. She argued that almost all of it could be traced back to medieval Catholic Europe, and that the idea of a mainly Aztec festival was largely a twentieth century story. Others, like the art historian Ruben Cordova, take a middle path. The candles, the wheat bread, the sugar and the churchyards came from Spain, he writes. The old story, often repeated, that kind-hearted priests deliberately moved the Aztec festival to November, to make conversion easier, has no real evidence behind it. The friars weren't trying to keep the old feasts. They were trying to end them. Now let's go into the city, to a small crowded print shop near the old centre, at the turn of the century.

The room smells of ink and oil and paper. There's a heavy iron press in the middle, and stacks of cheap coloured paper on the shelves, and long strings across the ceiling where freshly printed sheets hang to dry. His name is José Guadalupe Posada. He was born in Aguascalientes in 1852, and he's been making pictures for printers all his working life. Now he works for a publisher in Mexico City named Antonio Vanegas Arroyo, who prints all kinds of cheap broadsheets: songs, prayers, ghost stories, news of crimes and disasters, games for children, and, every November, sheets of calaveras.

Posada has made thousands of images for them. Many of his most famous ones are skeletons. Skeletons dancing, skeletons riding bicycles, skeletons selling newspapers, skeletons playing guitars at a party. Skeletons dressed as dandies, as generals, as housewives, as market vendors. They're lively, comic and full of movement, and they're meant to make people laugh. The verses printed beside them were written by others. But the pictures were his.

Around the year 1910, Posada drew a small picture of a woman's skull, wearing a hat.

It's a very large hat. An enormous wide fashionable hat of the kind that wealthy ladies in Paris and New York and Mexico City were wearing at the time, piled with flowers and topped with two great ostrich plumes. Beneath the hat, there's just a grinning skull, and the bones of the shoulders. That's all.

The picture was a joke about vanity, and about people who tried too hard to look European and fashionable. Underneath all the plumes and the finery, it says, we're all the same in the end.

Posada died in January 1913. The first printing we know of that picture came later that year, on a Day of the Dead broadsheet that called the lady a garbancera. A garbancera was a woman who sold chickpeas in the street. The verse beside the picture mocked such women for powdering their faces and dressing above their station. It wasn't a kind verse, and it wasn't Posada's.

For many years, the picture was just one among thousands.

One of those artists was the great muralist, Diego Rivera.

In 1946 and 1947, Rivera painted an enormous mural for a hotel in Mexico City, beside the Alameda park. It's called Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda. But now she has a whole body. She wears a long white dress. Around her shoulders, instead of a fashionable boa, there's a feathered serpent, the old Mesoamerican symbol. In the 1920s, the Day of the Dead began to be noticed in a new way.

Mexico was coming out of the long years of revolution, and its new governments, and its writers and artists, were searching for what it meant to be Mexican. The people of its shores are Purépecha, with their own language and their own long history. They bring candles and flowers, and food laid out on the graves.

In the 1920s, government officials came to see it. Photographers came, and writers. Pictures and articles appeared in newspapers and magazines, read by artists and anthropologists in Mexico and abroad. A historian of dance and performance, Ruth Hellier-Tinoco, has written about how the vigil, and a dance called the Dance of the Little Old Men, came to be presented as symbols of authentic Mexico in these years. Some things were staged for visitors. The fishermen of the lake, with their big butterfly-shaped nets, became famous in photographs, and the display of those nets is still performed for visitors today. But the family vigil in the island cemetery was, and is, real. It's simply that it became famous too.

The same thing happened, slowly, to the whole festival.

The government promoted the Day of the Dead as a national tradition, a symbol of Mexico's mixed and ancient heritage, and of its Indigenous roots in particular. Schools taught it. Artists painted it. In the capital, museums began to set up great public altars every November, the house museums of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo among them. Later in the century, from the 1970s onward, more promotion helped the urban colourful version of the festival spread into parts of Mexico where it had once been kept more quietly, or in other ways.

Across the northern border, in the United States, families of Mexican heritage had always kept their own Day of the Dead at home. But in the 1970s and eighties, artists and activists of the Chicano movement began to celebrate it publicly, in galleries and community centres in Los Angeles, and San Francisco, and San Antonio. Wherever it's kept, it isn't a night for frights. It's a night for welcoming people home. The Day of the Dead is, above all, a family's remembrance of its own dead.

UNESCO's description speaks of families laying petals and candles along the path from the cemetery to the home, preparing the dead person's favourite dishes, and setting them around the home altar and the tomb. This happens at the end of October and the beginning of November, when the year's maize harvest is coming to an end.

Some people find it a little unsettling to learn how much the festival was shaped in the last hundred years, by governments, and artists, and tourism, and the camera. Others find it reassuring. Over the last century, Mixquic became one of the most famous places in the country for these days. We can picture how it might have begun. There are many ways to build an ofrenda. Some families make one level, some two, some three, some seven. Some build an arch of cane over the top. There's no single right way. This family has always done it with two steps, because that's how Doña Elena's mother did it.

And then the fruit. Bananas, and apples, and guavas, and little mandarins, and lengths of sugar cane, laid out in heaps along the cloth. Sweet tamales, wrapped in their husks, pink inside. And two round loaves of pan de muerto, with their crossed strips of dough bones, dusted with sugar.

Long ago, people say, it was done with bonfires and with splinters of resinous pine, called ocote. Now it's candles.

The churchyard is already busy. Doña Elena sets her candle at the head of Don Andrés's grave, and lights it. Rosa takes more candles from the bag, and Lupe helps her set them all around the grave, in a ring, and lights them too, one by one, very carefully.

The sun goes down behind the hills. For a while, the sky is gold, and then rose, and then a soft violet. And all across the churchyard, the candles are coming alight, one grave after another, around the old church with its dark stone front. Soon the whole place is a field of small steady flames, and the marigolds glow in their light like embers.

They set up the chairs. They spread a blanket on the ground beside the grave for Lupe. And they settle in.

From the basket come pieces of sweet bread, wrapped in a cloth. Rosa pours the coffee into little cups, and passes them round. Doña Elena pours one extra cup, and sets it at the head of the grave, beside the candle.

There are visitors here too, a great many of them, from all over the city and much further away, walking slowly between the graves, speaking in low voices. Out in the streets beyond the wall, there are stalls, and lights, and from the plaza, every so often, a little music drifts over, from the festival held in these days. But inside the churchyard, around the graves, it's quieter.

At the next grave, an old couple sit close together under a blanket, not saying much. Two graves further on, a big family are eating and talking and laughing, children ducking between the crosses in the candlelight. Over by the church wall, a young woman sits alone beside a very new grave, with her hands in her lap, and her head bowed. Nobody disturbs her. A woman from the next family brings her a cup of coffee, and puts it beside her, and goes back to her own place.

That's how it is here. Grief, and laughter, and food, and quiet, all at once, all in the same candlelit churchyard.

At Don Andrés's grave, the family begins to tell stories about him. Martín remembers the time his father tried to fix the canoe with the wrong kind of glue, and it sank, very slowly, in the middle of the canal, with him still sitting in it, still holding the pole. Rosa remembers how he used to sing in the kitchen when he thought no one could hear him, always the same song, and always with the wrong words. Lupe remembers the fish. And Doña Elena, after a while, remembers the first time she ever saw him, fifty years ago, at a dance in the plaza, wearing a shirt that was much too big for him, borrowed from his older brother.

They laugh. And then they're quiet for a while. And Doña Elena reaches out, and puts her hand flat on the marigolds over the grave, and leaves it there.

"When I was a girl," she says, after a while, "my grandmother used to come back and light the candles again, eight days later. To make sure they'd got home safely." She smiles. "Now we just come on the second."

The night grows cooler. The sky above the churchyard is clear and dark, and full of stars. Here and there, people are praying quietly, in murmurs, the old words rising and falling like breathing.

Lupe has been trying very hard to stay awake. She's nine, and this is the first year she's been allowed to stay until the end. But the candlelight is warm and steady, and the voices are low, and the coffee was mostly milk. At some point, she climbs up into her grandmother's lap, though she's really much too big for it now, and Doña Elena wraps the rebozo around them both. And within a few minutes, Lupe is asleep.

Rosa drops a small piece of copal onto the coals in the little sahumador they've brought with them. The white smoke curls up, slow and sweet, and drifts across the grave, through the candlelight, and away between the crosses. All across the churchyard, there are other thin threads of smoke, rising into the still air, and the whole place smells of resin and wax and marigolds.

For a long time, nobody says anything at all. The candles flicker. A dog barks, far off, in the town, and stops. Doña Elena thinks about nothing in particular, about the sound of Don Andrés's footsteps in the yard in the mornings, about the smell of his straw hat, about the way he used to whistle to the birds. She doesn't feel sad, exactly. She feels as if he's very near.

As families say in many places, it's time now for the dead to go back. They've had their visit. They've been welcomed, and fed, and remembered, and told that they're loved. Next year, they'll come again.

Toward midnight, the families begin to gather their things. The church doors will close soon, and the churchyard will be cleared for the night. The candles are left to burn down where they stand. Martín folds the chairs. Rosa gathers the cups and the cloth into the basket. And Martín lifts Lupe, still asleep, onto his shoulder, and she doesn't wake.

Doña Elena stays a moment longer. She looks down at the grave, at the ring of small flames, and the heaps of orange flowers, and on the cross, freshly painted, her husband's name.

"Go well, viejo," she says.

Then they walk home together, slowly, through the dark streets, with the glow of the churchyard behind them.

In the morning, there's a thin mist on the canals. Lupe wakes up in her own bed, and can't remember how she got there. And then she remembers. She runs to the front room.

The ofrenda is still there, just as they left it. The candles have burned low. The marigolds are a little tired.

"Did he come?" she asks, very quietly.

Doña Elena takes her hand.

"I think so," she says. "I think he had a very nice time."

Then, together, they take the ofrenda down. The bread, the fruit, the tamales, are shared out onto plates, and wrapped in cloths. Lupe and her mother carry them through the streets to her godparents, and her aunts, and the neighbours, and come home with other plates in return. In Mixquic they call this dar la calavera, giving the skull. Nothing from the ofrenda is wasted. It's eaten, together, by the living.

2:00:02Goodnight · 373 words

It's evening again in Mixquic. The sky over the canals is turning from gold to violet.

In the churchyard around the old church of San Andrés, orange marigolds cover a grave. The candles are lit, one by one, and the petals glow. And across the town, in small front rooms, in the light of other candles, there are photographs, and plates of food, and glasses of water, and little sugar skulls with names written on them.

We've come a long way tonight. From Citlalin on the chinampas, offering flowers in the flower month, and setting out food for her husband on his long journey. To Ana in the new church courtyard, with her candles and her little clay bird. To the sugar lambs under the arcades, and the old women calling out, skulls, girls, skulls. To Doña Refugio at her stall, and Posada at his bench, and the lady in the great feathered hat. And at last, to Doña Elena, with her hand resting on the marigolds, and Lupe asleep in her lap.

Five hundred years, and more. Two worlds, joined together, not always easily, into one. And through all of it, the same simple wish. To remember the people we've loved. To set a place for them. To light a small light, so that they can find their way home.

Somewhere tonight, there are families sitting in churchyards beside their dead, in the warm light of candles, with a thermos of something hot, and a blanket around the shoulders, telling the old stories one more time. Somewhere a child is asleep in a grandmother's lap. Somewhere a bell is ringing in the dark, and children are running from door to door. Somewhere a candle is being set, very carefully, beside a photograph.

Let the candles burn low now. Let the marigolds glow in the dark. Let the bells ring slowly over the old town, and the mist come in across the canals.

There's nothing more to do tonight. The table is laid. The path of petals leads to the door. The names are written on the little sugar skulls, in pink and turquoise and gold. Everyone who is remembered has been remembered.

And let yourself rest.

Goodnight. Until next time, sleep well.
